decks.name: Small Town Campaign Start
decks.description: A grounded beginning for a party that starts life in a quiet frontier town. Most of the cards go into the bonds between the characters and the texture of the place they call home, then a few institutions, rivalries, and half-buried secrets are salted in. By the end you should have a town that feels lived-in, a web of relationships the players actually care about, and two or three loose threads the GM can pull on whenever the campaign needs a direction.
focus: Build connections between characters.
Define what makes the town unique.
Seed a few unresolved problems.
Leave two or three adventure hooks.

decks.name: Political Intrigue
decks.description: A campaign of nobles, guilds, and shifting alliances where the sharpest weapon is information. The deck front-loads political tensions and the organizations that embody them, gives those factions faces the players know personally, and deliberately avoids clean sides. Expect competing interests, useful enemies, and allies who may not stay allies.

decks.name: Merchant Guild Campaign
decks.description: For a party whose fortunes rise and fall with commerce, exploration, and trade. The deck emphasizes the economy, the guilds and companies that move goods, and the opportunities worth chasing, with a thread of travel and politics to keep the money entangled with the world. You should come away with valuable goods, contested trade routes, influential merchants, and rivals who want what you have.

decks.name: Frontier Exploration
decks.description: A newly settled region where the map still has blank spaces and every landmark hides a story. The deck weights wilderness, the opportunities a frontier offers, and the fragile communities clinging to it, threaded with travel and the deep history buried underfoot. Use it to define landmarks, mark out the dangerous places, and seed the ancient ruins the party will eventually be foolish enough to enter.

decks.name: Kingdom at War
decks.description: The campaign opens with two nations already at each other's throats and the party caught in the middle. The deck spends its weight on conflict, the politics driving it, and the history that made it inevitable, while keeping the relationships that give the war personal stakes. It leaves room for diplomacy as much as battle, and asks why this war matters to these characters in particular.

decks.name: Mystery Campaign
decks.description: Everything here bends toward a single unknown truth. The deck is dominated by mystery and the history it's rooted in, with just enough people, factions, and politics to give the questions somewhere to live. It is built to produce conflicting theories rather than tidy answers, so the table ends up with a knot worth spending a campaign untangling.

decks.name: Gods and Mortals
decks.description: A campaign where faith is a force in the world rather than a detail on a character sheet. The deck leans on religion and the divine signs that come with it, then gives those beliefs institutions, histories, and people who disagree about what any of it means. It stays deliberately open about whether the gods are real, present, or worth following, so the table can land anywhere from devout to heretical without the deck deciding first.
focus: Establish what people believe and why.
Give the faith a body: temples, orders, and authorities.
Leave the truth of the divine unsettled.

decks.name: An Age of Magic
decks.description: For a world where magic is common enough to shape daily life and strange enough that nobody fully understands it. The deck is weighted toward the mystical and the questions magic leaves behind, then anchors it with the traditions, circles, and long histories that decide who gets to practise. Use it whether magic in your world is a gift, a science, an inheritance, or a slow-burning problem.

decks.name: The Arcane Engine
decks.description: A world where magic has been industrialised — bottled, sold, wired into cities, and put to work. The deck splits its weight between the mystical and the economy that has grown around it, then adds the companies, laws, and street-level habits that follow any new industry. Expect questions about who owns the enchantment, who is exposed to its waste, and what the old practitioners think of all this.

decks.name: City Underworld
decks.description: A street-level campaign in a city where the real authority is not the one on the letterhead. The deck spends most of its weight on the crews and syndicates that run things, the money moving between them, and the personal debts that hold it all together. Where Political Intrigue works the court, this one works the alley — but the syndicates still have reach beyond the walls.

decks.name: Under Occupation
decks.description: The war is over and your side lost. The deck weights the friction of living under someone else's authority, the politics that put them there, and the question of who the characters are now that the old order is gone — then gives the resistance a shape and a set of people worth protecting. It assumes the party is on the losing side and asks what they are willing to do about it.

decks.name: Mythic Age
decks.description: For a campaign that starts where most campaigns end — with characters who already matter to the world and problems measured in ages rather than seasons. This is the only deck that draws on world-defining cards, so expect prophecies, ancient enemies, and the kind of history that gets sung rather than remembered. Best used for a high-level start or a returning party whose reputation arrived before they did.

decks.name: Village at the Wild's Edge
decks.description: A small-village beginning for a land that never got tamed. The bones are the same as a quiet frontier start — who these people are to each other, and what the village is actually like to live in — but half the deck is given over to the country around it and the older things living in that country. Ilyndor does not treat a village as the centre of anything. By the end you should have neighbours worth protecting, a stretch of wild the village has learned to be careful about, and at least one thing out there that was here long before the first roof went up.
